lessons.title: Mnemonics & Memory Tricks
lessons.summary: Recall qualitative-analysis patterns fast.

blocks.markdown:
## Essential memory hooks

- **A–Z**: aluminium and zinc hydroxides dissolve in excess sodium hydroxide.
- **ZnCu**: zinc and copper(II) precipitates dissolve in excess ammonia.
- **GRB**: iron(II) green, iron(III) red-brown, copper(II) blue.

Who dissolves in excess NaOH?

A–Z

A = Al³⁺ Z = Zn²⁺

"A to Z" — Al³⁺ and Zn²⁺ give a white ppt that dissolves in excess NaOH to form a colourless solution. Every other hydroxide stays insoluble in excess NaOH.

Who dissolves in excess NH₃?

ZnCu

Zn²⁺ → colourless Cu²⁺ → DARK BLUE

"Zoo Creatures dissolve" — Only Zn²⁺ and Cu²⁺ dissolve in excess NH₃. Cu²⁺ gives a stunning DARK BLUE solution — easiest to spot!

Coloured precipitates (not white)

GRB

G = Fe²⁺ (Green) R = Fe³⁺ (Red-brown) B = Cu²⁺ (Light blue)

"Get Rusty Blue" — Fe²⁺ is Green (young iron), Fe³⁺ is Red-Brown (rusty iron), Cu²⁺ is Light Blue. Everything else is WHITE.

Ca²⁺ is the odd one out

Ca = NaOH ONLY

White ppt with NaOH ✓ No ppt with NH₃ ✗

Calcium is "fussy" — it only reacts with NaOH, not NH₃. Use this to distinguish Ca²⁺ from the other white-ppt ions.

NH₄⁺ is special — no precipitate!

NH₄⁺ → GAS

NaOH + warm → NH₃ gas Turns moist red litmus BLUE

"Ammonium doesn't precipitate — it evaporates!" Add NaOH and warm. Colourless, pungent gas turns moist red litmus paper blue = NH₄⁺ confirmed.

Gas Tests — 3 pairs

Splint · Litmus · Bubble

H₂ = lighted splint, POP O₂ = glowing splint relights

NH₃ = red litmus → blue Cl₂ = blue litmus → red, bleached

CO₂ = limewater white ppt SO₂ = KMnO₄ purple → colourless

Think of gas tests as 3 pairs: splint tests (H₂, O₂), litmus tests (NH₃, Cl₂), and bubble-through tests (CO₂, SO₂).

Quick-Fire Rules

Rule 1: A–Z dissolves in excess NaOH

Al³⁺ and Zn²⁺ — white ppt first, then dissolves in excess NaOH to give a colourless solution.

Rule 2: Only Zn²⁺ dissolves in BOTH

Zn²⁺ dissolves in excess NaOH AND excess NH₃. Use this to distinguish Zn²⁺ from Al³⁺.

Rule 3: Cu²⁺ = Dark Blue in NH₃

Light blue ppt first, then a dark blue solution in excess NH₃ — it's Cu²⁺. 100% guaranteed.

Rule 4: Strong vs weak alkali

NaOH ionises completely: NaOH(aq) → Na⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq). NH₃ ionises partially: NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq).

Rule 5: Acidify before Ag⁺ or Ba²⁺

Anion tests involve acidification — add dilute nitric acid first so CO₃²⁻ and OH⁻ don't give false positive white precipitates.

Rule 6: Two tests give NH₃ gas

NH₄⁺ + NaOH (warm) AND NO₃⁻ + NaOH + Al foil (warm) both evolve ammonia gas that turns moist red litmus paper blue.

rows: Light blue precipitate; dissolves to dark blue

blocks.markdown:
What's happening: Tests for cations involve alkalis (aqueous sodium hydroxide and aqueous ammonia), which ionise in water to produce hydroxide (OH⁻) ions. The hydroxide ions react with most metal cations to produce metal hydroxides.

Complete ionisation of NaOH in water:

NaOH(aq) → Na⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)

Partial ionisation of NH₃ in water:

NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)

Identify cations based on: ① Formation of a precipitate (if any) when a few drops of alkali are added → ② Colour of the precipitate formed (if any) → ③ Solubility of the precipitate (if any) in excess alkali

lessons.summary: Identify common anions with controlled reagent sequences.

blocks.markdown:
## Halides

Acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous silver nitrate:

- chloride: white precipitate
- bromide: cream precipitate
- iodide: yellow precipitate

blocks.title: Avoid false positives
blocks.body: Acidify before silver nitrate or barium nitrate tests. Carbonates and hydroxides otherwise interfere.

figures.caption: Original anion and gas-test reference poster

blocks.markdown:
The approach: Tests for anions involve acidification, followed by evolution of gas or precipitation. Adding dilute nitric acid first removes CO₃²⁻ and OH⁻ that would give false positive white precipitates.

AnionTestObservation

Carbonate (CO₃²⁻)

Add dilute acid. Bubble gas through limewater (aqueous calcium hydroxide).

Effervescence of a colourless and odourless gas is observed. White precipitate of CaCO₃ is produced when gas is bubbled through limewater.

Chloride (Cl⁻)

Add dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous silver nitrate.

White precipitate of AgCl is produced.

Iodide (I⁻)

Add dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous silver nitrate.

Yellow precipitate of AgI is produced.

Sulfate (SO₄²⁻)

Add dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous barium nitrate.

White precipitate of BaSO₄ is produced.

Nitrate (NO₃⁻)

Add aqueous sodium hydroxide and a small piece of aluminium foil. Warm the mixture.

Colourless and pungent ammonia gas that turns moist red litmus paper blue is evolved when warmed.

Distinguishing Cl⁻ vs I⁻

Cl⁻ — Chloride

Dilute HNO₃ + AgNO₃(aq) → White ppt (AgCl)

I⁻ — Iodide

Dilute HNO₃ + AgNO₃(aq) → Yellow ppt (AgI)

Same reagent, different colour: Cl⁻ and I⁻ use the exact same test (dilute nitric acid, then aqueous silver nitrate). Only the precipitate colour tells them apart — white for chloride, yellow for iodide.

GasTestObservation

Hydrogen (H₂)

Place a lighted splint at the mouth of the test tube.

Colourless and odourless gas extinguishes the lighted splint with a "pop" sound

Oxygen (O₂)

Insert a glowing splint into the test tube.

Colourless and odourless gas relights the glowing splint

Carbon dioxide (CO₂)

Bubble the gas through limewater (aqueous calcium hydroxide).

Colourless and odourless gas produces a white precipitate of CaCO₃

Ammonia (NH₃)

Place a piece of moist red litmus paper at the mouth of the test tube.

Colourless and pungent gas turns moist red litmus paper BLUE

Chlorine (Cl₂)

Place a piece of moist blue litmus paper at the mouth of the test tube.

Yellow-green and pungent gas turns moist blue litmus paper red and eventually bleaches it

Sulfur dioxide (SO₂)

Bubble the gas through aqueous acidified potassium manganate(VII).

Colourless and pungent gas turns aqueous acidified KMnO₄ from purple to colourless

Gas Memory Groups:

Splint tests: H₂ (lighted splint, POP) | O₂ (glowing splint relights)

Litmus tests: NH₃ (moist red → blue) | Cl₂ (moist blue → red, then bleached)

Bubble-through tests: CO₂ (limewater → white ppt) | SO₂ (acidified KMnO₄ → colourless)

Easy Confusions

NH₃ vs Cl₂

Both are pungent! NH₃ is colourless and turns moist RED litmus blue. Cl₂ is yellow-green and turns moist BLUE litmus red, then bleaches it.

H₂ vs O₂

Both are colourless and odourless! H₂ uses a LIGHTED splint (pop sound). O₂ uses a GLOWING splint (relights).

CO₂ vs SO₂

Both bubble-through tests! CO₂ is odourless (limewater → white ppt). SO₂ is pungent (KMnO₄ purple → colourless).

lessons.title: QA Strategy — Systematic Approach
lessons.summary: Choose salt preparation method from solubility and reactants.

items.title: Insoluble salt
items.body: Precipitation: mix two soluble solutions, filter, wash, then dry.

items.title: Soluble salt from acid + insoluble base
items.body: Add excess solid, filter, then crystallise.

items.title: Soluble Group 1 or ammonium salt
items.body: Titration: use exact neutralisation, then crystallise.

blocks.markdown:
What is QA? Qualitative analysis is a method used to identify elements and/or compounds present in an unknown substance, using physical tests (based on pH, smell, colour and solubility) and chemical tests (identification of cations, anions and gases).

Step 1 — Physical ObservationLook at the colour of the solid and the solution. Coloured solutions → transition metal (Fe²⁺, Fe³⁺, Cu²⁺). White solid, colourless solution → Ca²⁺, Al³⁺, Zn²⁺, NH₄⁺

↓

Step 2 — Add NaOH dropwise, then in excess

Green ppt → Fe²⁺

Red-brown ppt → Fe³⁺

Light blue ppt → Cu²⁺

White ppt → Ca²⁺, Al³⁺ or Zn²⁺

No ppt, gas on warming → NH₄⁺

For white ppt: does it dissolve in excess NaOH? → A–Z (Al³⁺, Zn²⁺). Insoluble → Ca²⁺

↓

Step 3 — Add NH₃ dropwise, then in excess (to confirm)

Light blue ppt, dark blue solution in excess → Cu²⁺ ✓

White ppt dissolves in excess → Zn²⁺ (Al³⁺ stays insoluble)

No ppt at all → Ca²⁺

↓

Step 4 — Test for AnionsAcidify with dilute nitric acid first! Then aqueous barium nitrate (for SO₄²⁻), aqueous silver nitrate (for Cl⁻ / I⁻), dilute acid alone + limewater (for CO₃²⁻), NaOH + Al foil + warm (for NO₃⁻)

↓

Step 5 — Test any evolved gasesMatch gas colour + smell + specific test → identify H₂, O₂, CO₂, NH₃, Cl₂ or SO₂

Distinguishing Similar Ions

Pair to DistinguishKey TestResult

Al³⁺ vs Zn²⁺Add excess NH₃Only Zn²⁺ dissolves in excess NH₃ to form a colourless solution. Al³⁺ remains as a white ppt.

Ca²⁺ vs Al³⁺ / Zn²⁺Add NH₃Ca²⁺ gives NO precipitate with NH₃ at all. Al³⁺ and Zn²⁺ give white ppt.

Fe²⁺ vs Fe³⁺Colour of ppt with NaOH / NH₃Fe²⁺ = green ppt. Fe³⁺ = red-brown ppt. Both insoluble in excess.

NH₄⁺ vs other cationsAdd NaOH + warmNH₄⁺ gives NO ppt, but colourless pungent gas (NH₃) that turns moist red litmus paper blue.

Cl⁻ vs I⁻Dilute HNO₃ + AgNO₃(aq)Cl⁻ = white ppt (AgCl). I⁻ = yellow ppt (AgI).

SO₄²⁻ vs CO₃²⁻Add dilute acidCO₃²⁻ gives effervescence of CO₂ (white ppt with limewater). SO₄²⁻ does not react with dilute acid.

lessons.title: Laboratory Methods of Preparing Salts
lessons.summary: Select precipitation, filtration, or titration.

blocks.title: Decide the method
blocks.body: Method depends on the salt's **solubility in water**. First ask whether the product salt is soluble. If it is, ask whether its starting materials are soluble.

items.title: Insoluble product
items.body: Use **precipitation**: mix two soluble aqueous salts, then filter, wash, and dry the precipitate.

items.title: Soluble product; insoluble reactant
items.body: Use **excess solid + acid**: filter away leftover solid, then crystallise the salt from the filtrate.

items.title: Soluble product; soluble reactants
items.body: Use **titration**: find the exact neutralisation volume, then repeat without indicator before crystallising.

blocks.markdown:
A **precipitate** is an insoluble product. Mix one soluble salt supplying the required cation with another supplying the required anion.

1. Mix the two aqueous solutions and stir until no more precipitate forms.
2. Filter: keep the **residue** (the precipitate), discard the filtrate.
3. Wash the residue with deionised water to remove soluble reactants.
4. Dry it between sheets of filter paper.

Use a warm dilute acid with an **excess** moderately reactive metal, insoluble base, or insoluble carbonate. Warm metals and insoluble bases; carbonates react readily without heating.

1. Add excess solid to the acid and stir until reaction stops.
2. Filter to remove unused solid; keep the filtrate.
3. Heat the filtrate to the point of saturation — **do not evaporate to dryness**.
4. Cool so crystals form, then filter.
5. Wash crystals with a small amount of **cold** deionised water and dry them.

Excess solid ensures all acid reacts; filtration removes the leftover solid.

rows: Mg, Al, Zn, or Fe — moderately reactive metals
MgO, ZnO, CuO, Fe(OH)₃, or Cu(OH)₂

blocks.title: Choose reactants carefully
blocks.body: Do not use unreactive metals such as lead or copper, or very reactive sodium, potassium, or calcium. Do not use this method for insoluble salts: a solid product can coat the reactant and stop the reaction. Use precipitation instead.

blocks.text: Titration — soluble Group 1 or ammonium salts

blocks.markdown:
Group 1 and ammonium salts need an acid plus alkali. Both reactants are soluble, so nothing can be filtered away.

**First titration — find the volume.** Pipette 25.0 cm³ of alkali into a conical flask, add 2–3 drops of indicator, then run acid from a burette to the permanent endpoint. Record the acid volume used.

**Repeat without indicator.** Use the same acid volume but omit the indicator so crystals stay pure. Heat to saturation, cool to crystallise, filter the crystals, rinse with a little cold deionised water, and dry them.

blocks.markdown:
The big idea: The method of salt preparation depends on the salt's solubility in water. Ask two questions in order: ① Is the salt soluble? ② Are the starting materials soluble?

Q1 — Is the salt to be prepared soluble in water?

NO → Insoluble salt → Method (A) Precipitation

YES → Soluble salt → go to Q2

↓

Q2 — Are the starting materials for making the salt soluble in water?

NO (Non-SPA salts) → Method (B) Filtration — acid + excess insoluble reactant

YES (SPA salts — Group 1 or ammonium cations) → Method (C) Titration

Method (A) — Precipitation (Insoluble Salts)

A precipitate is an insoluble chemical produced during a chemical reaction. ALL insoluble salts can be prepared by the precipitation method. Mix a soluble salt (e.g. a nitrate) containing the cation with a soluble salt (e.g. a sodium salt) containing the anion.

Steps: Add one aqueous solution to the other aqueous solution → Stir thoroughly until no more precipitate forms → Filter and collect the residue (which contains the precipitate); discard the filtrate → Wash the residue with deionised water to remove unwanted reactants → Dry the residue between sheets of filter paper.

Method (B) — Filtration (Soluble Salts NOT containing Group 1 / Ammonium)

React warm dilute acid with an excess insoluble reactant: a moderately reactive metal, an insoluble base, or an insoluble carbonate. Warm only when using a metal or insoluble base — carbonates react quickly, so no heating is needed.

Steps: Add excess reactant to warm dilute acid, stir until no more reacts → Filter the mixture to obtain the filtrate → Heat the filtrate till the point of saturation ( CANNOT evaporate to dryness — crystals will decompose upon heating) → Test for saturation by dipping a glass rod into the solution (optional) → Cool the filtrate to allow crystals to form → Filter to obtain the crystals as residue → Wash with a small amount of COLD deionised water → Dry crystals between pieces of filter paper.

Why excess? To ensure ALL the acid is completely used up — the leftover insoluble reactant is easily removed by filtration.

CombinationExamples of reactants

Acid + metalMg, Al, Zn, Fe (moderately reactive metals only)

Acid + insoluble baseMgO, ZnO, CuO, Fe(OH)₃, Cu(OH)₂

Acid + insoluble carbonateMgCO₃, ZnCO₃, CuCO₃

Acids usedHCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄

✗ The acid + metal method is NOT suitable for:

• Unreactive metals — lead and copper do not react with dilute acids

• Very reactive metals — sodium, potassium and calcium react too vigorously (explosive!)

• Making salts that are insoluble in water — e.g. PbCl₂, PbSO₄, AgCl (use precipitation instead)

✗ The PbCl₂ trap: Can we make PbCl₂ via PbO(s) + 2HCl(aq) → PbCl₂(s) + H₂O(l)? NO! If the product starts off as a solid, it will not fully react to completion — the insoluble PbCl₂ layer coats the PbO and stops the reaction. Insoluble salts like PbCl₂ must be made by precipitation.

Method (C) — Titration (Group 1 or Ammonium Salts)

Soluble salts containing Group 1 or ammonium cations are prepared by reacting an acid with an alkali (or a carbonate solution). Both starting materials are soluble, so nothing can be filtered off — a titration must first find the exact volume of acid that neutralises a known volume of alkali. Sodium, potassium and ammonium salts are prepared using the titration method.

Part 1 (with indicator): Fill a burette with the dilute acid; note the initial reading (V₁ cm³) → Pipette 25.0 cm³ of aqueous alkali into a conical flask → Add 2 to 3 drops of an indicator (e.g. phenolphthalein or methyl orange) → Add the acid slowly from the burette until the endpoint, where ONE drop of acid causes the indicator to change colour permanently → Record the final reading (V₂ cm³). Volume of acid needed for complete neutralisation = (V₂ − V₁) cm³.

Part 2 (without indicator): Repeat the titration WITHOUT the indicator — the indicator would make the salt impure — by adding the same volume (V₂ − V₁) cm³ of acid → Transfer to a crucible and heat to evaporate the water to form a saturated solution (glass rod test: crystals form on the cool rod = saturated) → Cool the hot saturated solution so the salt can crystallise → Filter to obtain the crystals and rinse with a little cold deionised water → Dry by pressing between sheets of filter paper.

Bar length = how violently the metal reacts with dilute acid. K, Na, Ca: too dangerous — never used for salt prep. Mg → Fe: the safe "acid + excess metal" zone. Sn, Pb: too slow / self-coating. Below H: no reaction ever — go via the oxide, hydroxide or carbonate.

Worked Examples from the Handout

(a) Acid + Metal — Zinc sulfate

Zn(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + H₂(g)

Dissolve (excess zinc, constant stirring) → Filter (remove unreacted zinc) → Concentrate (evaporate to about one-third the original volume) → Crystallise (cool to room temperature) → Filter, wash, dry.

(b) Acid + Insoluble Base — Copper(II) sulfate

CuO(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → CuSO₄(aq) + H₂O(l)

Add CuO to sulfuric acid until no more can dissolve → filter to remove excess CuO (residue) → concentrate, crystallise, filter the filtrate → copper(II) sulfate crystals.

(c) Acid + Carbonate — Calcium nitrate

CaCO₃(s) + 2HNO₃(aq) → Ca(NO₃)₂(aq) + CO₂(g) + H₂O(l)

Carbonates react quickly with acids, so no heating is needed. Add calcium carbonate until no more dissolves → filter → concentrate, crystallise, filter.

lessons.title: Types of Oxides
lessons.summary: Classify oxides by reaction with acids and bases.

items.title: Basic oxides
items.body: Usually metal oxides; react with acids.

items.title: Acidic oxides
items.body: Usually non-metal oxides; react with bases.

items.title: Amphoteric oxides
items.body: React with both acids and bases; aluminium oxide is an example.

items.title: Neutral oxides
items.body: Do not show acid-base behaviour; carbon monoxide is an example.

blocks.markdown:
The quick sort: Metal + oxygen → usually a basic oxide. Non-metal + oxygen → usually an acidic oxide. Then learn the two exception clubs: the amphoteric trio (metal oxides that swing both ways) and the neutral trio (non-metal oxides that react with nothing).

ACIDIC Oxides

Oxides of NON-METALS

Reacts with: bases / alkalis → salt + water

In water: many dissolve to form acids

Examples: CO₂ (→ carbonic acid), SO₂ (→ sulfurous acid), SO₃ (→ sulfuric acid), NO₂

SiO₂ is acidic but insoluble in water

Links to QA: CO₂ and SO₂ are your acidic gases — they turn damp blue litmus red.

BASIC Oxides

Oxides of METALS

Reacts with: acids → salt + water

In water: a few dissolve to form alkalis (Na₂O, K₂O, CaO)

Examples: Na₂O, K₂O, CaO, MgO, CuO, Fe₂O₃

Most (MgO, CuO, Fe₂O₃) are insoluble — perfect excess reactants for salt prep!

e.g. CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O — the filtration method classic.

AMPHOTERIC Oxides

Metal oxides that react BOTH ways

Reacts with: BOTH acids AND bases → salt + water

The most common three:

Al₂O₃ — aluminium oxide

ZnO — zinc oxide

PbO — lead(II) oxide

e.g. ZnO + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂O

and ZnO + 2NaOH → Na₂ZnO₂ + H₂O

Same A–Z–P trio as the amphoteric hydroxides in QA — Al and Zn are exactly why those white ppts dissolve in excess NaOH!

NEUTRAL Oxides

Non-metal oxides that react with NOTHING

Reacts with: neither acids nor bases

Effect on litmus: none — neutral to indicators

The most common three:

CO — carbon monoxide

NO — nitrogen monoxide

H₂O — water

Trap: CO is neutral but CO₂ is acidic; NO is neutral but NO₂ is acidic. One extra oxygen flips the type!

Classifying an Oxide — Decision Path

Q1 — Is it a metal oxide or non-metal oxide?

METAL → basic… unless it's Al₂O₃ / ZnO / PbO → amphoteric

NON-METAL → acidic… unless it's CO / NO / H₂O → neutral

↓

Q2 — Confirm by reaction

Reacts with acid only → BASIC

Reacts with alkali only → ACIDIC

Reacts with BOTH → AMPHOTERIC

Reacts with NEITHER → NEUTRAL

Memory hooks: Amphoteric = "A Zany Plumber" (Al₂O₃, ZnO, PbO). Neutral = "CO NO H₂O" — say it out loud, it almost rhymes ("see-oh, en-oh, aitch-two-oh"). Everything else follows the metal/non-metal rule.

lessons.title: Chemical Bonding & Structure
lessons.summary: Connect structure and bonding to material properties.

items.title: Ionic
items.body: Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. Conducts when molten or aqueous.

items.title: Simple molecular
items.body: Strong covalent bonds within molecules, weak forces between them. Low melting points.

items.title: Giant covalent
items.body: Many covalent bonds in a lattice. High melting points.

items.title: Metallic
items.body: Positive ions and delocalised electrons. Conducts electricity.

blocks.markdown:
The big idea: Chemical bonding occurs in both elements and compounds. Most atoms bond to achieve a stable (usually duplet or octet) electronic configuration with a completely filled valence electron shell, similar to noble gases. ALL types of chemical bonding involve electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged particles.

Types of Chemical Bonding and Structure

Property

IONIC

Giant ionic lattice

COVALENT

Simple molecular

COVALENT

Giant covalent

METALLIC

Giant metallic lattice

Description

Electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions

Electrostatic forces of attraction between the positively charged nuclei of atoms and their shared pair(s) of electrons

Electrostatic forces of attraction between metal cations and sea of delocalised valence electrons

Formation

Metal atoms transfer their valence electrons to non-metal atoms

Two atoms share at least one pair of valence electrons

Metal atoms lose valence electrons to form metal cations surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons that can move freely between the cations

Particles

Oppositely charged ions in a regular lattice

Simple (discrete) molecules

Extensive network of atoms

Lattice of metal cations + sea of delocalised valence electrons

Melting & boiling points

High — large amount of thermal energy required to overcome the strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions

Low — only a small amount of thermal energy required to overcome the weak intermolecular forces of attraction between molecules

High — large amount of thermal energy required to break all the strong covalent bonds between atoms in the extensive network

High (except Group 1 metals and mercury) — large amount of thermal energy required to overcome the strong electrostatic forces between metal cations and the sea of delocalised electrons

Conducts electricity?

✓ Yes in molten and aqueous states (free-moving ions act as mobile charge carriers)

✗ No in all physical states (except acids and alkalis, which ionise in water)

✗ No in all physical states (except graphite)

✓ Yes in solid and molten states (delocalised valence electrons act as mobile charge carriers)

Solubility

Mostly soluble in water; insoluble in organic solvents

Mostly insoluble in water; soluble in organic solvents

Insoluble in water and organic solvents

Insoluble in water and organic solvents

Others

Hard and brittle

NIL

Hard (diamond, silicon dioxide); slippery (graphite)

High thermal conductivity; high density (except Group 1 metals); malleable and ductile

Giant Covalent Substances — Diamond vs Graphite

Diamond

Hard — all the carbon atoms are held rigidly in fixed positions by strong covalent bonds, which cannot be broken easily.

Does NOT conduct electricity — each carbon atom forms covalent bonds with FOUR other carbon atoms. All the valence electrons are used for bonding, so there are no delocalised electrons to act as mobile charge carriers.

Graphite

Slippery — each layer of carbon atoms can slide over another layer easily due to the weak intermolecular forces of attraction between the layers.

CAN conduct electricity — each carbon atom only uses THREE out of four valence electrons for covalent bonding, leaving one delocalised valence electron per carbon atom. These move freely along the layers as mobile charge carriers.

Deducing the Bonding and Structure of a Substance

Start — Melting and boiling points?

LOW → Simple covalent substances OR some metals (Group 1 metals or mercury)

HIGH → Giant lattice structures (metals / ionic compounds) OR giant covalent substances

↓

If LOW — Conducts electricity?

No, in all physical states → Simple covalent substance (check physical state at r.t.p.: solid e.g. sulfur, iodine · liquid e.g. water, bromine · gas e.g. oxygen, methane)

Yes, in aqueous state only → Simple covalent substance (acidic or alkaline gas, e.g. hydrogen chloride, ammonia)

Yes, in solid and molten states → Group 1 metal or mercury

↓

If HIGH — Conducts electricity in molten state?

No → Giant covalent substance (except graphite)

Yes → Giant lattice structure → then ask: conducts in SOLID state? Yes → Metal. No → Ionic compound

Pure Metals vs Alloys

Pure Metals

Atoms are arranged regularly in layers. When a force is applied, the layers of metal atoms can slide over each other easily. Hence pure metals are malleable (can be bent or flattened into thin sheets) and ductile (can be pulled into wires without breaking).

Alloys

An alloy is a solid mixture of a metal and one or a few other elements. The constituent atoms have different sizes, which disrupt the regular arrangement of atoms. A larger force is required to make the layers slide over each other, so an alloy is stronger and harder than a pure metal.

blocks.markdown:
Every fill-in-the-blank from the Bonding Concept Maps (I) & (II), plus the Salt Preparation exercises from Handout 2, with model answers. The completed responses are shown below for review.

Concept Map (I) — A. Ionic Bonding

Ionic bonds are formed when metal atoms transfer their valence electrons to non-metal atoms, allowing these atoms to achieve a stable octet / duplet electronic configuration. Metal cations and non-metal anions are formed as a result.

Ionic bonding is defined as the electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions in an ionic compound.

The ions in an ionic compound are arranged in a giant ionic (crystal) lattice structure, where the oppositely charged ions are arranged in a regular pattern.

The ions are held in place by strong electrostatic forces of attraction.

Concept Map (I) — B. Covalent Bonding

Covalent bonds are formed when two non-metal atoms share at least one pair of valence electrons, allowing both atoms to achieve a stable duplet / octet electronic configuration.

Covalent bonding is defined as the electrostatic forces of attraction between the positively charged nuclei of atoms and their shared pair(s) of electrons.

Simple covalent substances have a simple molecular structure and exist as simple (discrete) molecules held together by weak intermolecular forces of attraction. However, within each molecule, atoms are held together by strong covalent bonds.

Concept Map (I) — C. Physical Properties

Melting and boiling points: Ionic compounds — high. Simple covalent substances — low.

Electrical conductivity: Ionic compounds conduct electricity in aqueous and molten states. Simple covalent substances do not conduct electricity in any state.

Solubility: Most ionic compounds are soluble in water and insoluble in organic solvents. Most simple covalent substances are insoluble in water and soluble in organic solvents.

Others (ionic compounds): Brittle (will break apart easily when hit) and Hard (resistant to scratching or wear and tear).

Concept Map (II) — Particles in Each Structure

Giant ionic lattice: oppositely charged ions arranged in a regular lattice structure.

Simple molecular: simple (discrete) molecules.

Giant covalent: extensive network of atoms.

Giant metallic lattice: lattice of metal cations surrounded by a sea of delocalised valence electrons.

Concept Map (II) — Bonding Present

Ionic compounds: Ionic bonding (electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions).

Simple molecular: Covalent bonding (electrostatic forces of attraction between the positively charged nuclei of atoms and their shared pair(s) of electrons) between atoms, AND weak intermolecular forces of attraction between molecules.

Giant covalent: covalent bonding (electrostatic forces of attraction between the positively charged nuclei of atoms and their shared pair(s) of electrons) between atoms. Examples: diamond, graphite.

Metals: Metallic bonding (electrostatic forces of attraction between the metal cations and sea of delocalised valence electrons).

Concept Map (II) — Melting and Boiling Points

Giant ionic lattice: A large amount of thermal energy is needed to overcome the strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions. High melting and boiling points.

Simple molecular: Only a small amount of thermal energy is needed to overcome the weak intermolecular forces of attraction between molecules. Low melting and boiling points.

Giant covalent: A large amount of thermal energy is needed to break the strong covalent bonds between atoms. High melting and boiling points.

Giant metallic lattice: A large amount of thermal energy is needed to overcome the strong electrostatic forces of attraction between metal cations and sea of delocalised valence electrons. High melting and boiling points.

Concept Map (II) — Electrical Conductivity

Giant ionic lattice: Do not conduct electricity in solid state — ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice structure. Conduct electricity in molten and aqueous states — free-moving ions can act as mobile charge carriers to conduct electricity.

Simple molecular: Do not conduct electricity in any state — electrically neutral overall. Exceptions: acidic and alkaline gases, which ionise to produce free-moving ions when dissolved in water (e.g. ammonia and hydrogen chloride).

Giant covalent: Do not conduct electricity in any state — all valence electrons in the atoms are used for bonding. Exception: graphite — contains delocalised valence electrons that can move freely along the layers and act as mobile charge carriers to conduct electricity.

Giant metallic lattice: Conduct electricity in solid and molten states — contains delocalised valence electrons that can act as mobile charge carriers to conduct electricity.

Concept Map (II) — Solubility

Giant ionic lattice: mostly soluble in water, insoluble in organic solvents.

Simple molecular: mostly insoluble in water, soluble in organic solvents.

Giant covalent and giant metallic: insoluble in both water and organic solvents.

Concept Map (II) — Other Properties

Giant ionic lattice: Brittle (break apart easily when hit) and Hard (resistant to wear and tear).

Giant covalent: Hard — all the atoms are held rigidly in fixed positions by strong covalent bonds, which cannot be broken easily. Exception: graphite — consists of flat layers of carbon atoms that can slide over another layer easily, making it soft and slippery.

Giant metallic lattice: High thermal conductivity, high density, malleable (can be bent or flattened into thin sheets when hammered), ductile (can be pulled into wires without breaking), shiny, sonorous.

Exam technique: The three bonding definitions all follow the same template — "electrostatic forces of attraction between ___ and ___". Ionic: oppositely charged ions. Covalent: positively charged nuclei + shared pair(s) of electrons. Metallic: metal cations + sea of delocalised valence electrons. Learn the template once, swap in the particles.

Salt Preparation — Ex 1: Acid + Metal / Base / Carbonate (Handout p12)

Suggest the reagents required to prepare the following soluble salts by the filtration method. The anion decides the acid, the cation decides the metal / base / carbonate — and check the reactivity series before picking a metal!

(a) Copper(II) sulfate: dilute sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄) + excess copper(II) oxide / copper(II) carbonate — NOT copper metal, it is below hydrogen and does not react with dilute acids.

(b) Iron(II) chloride: dilute hydrochloric acid (HCl) + excess iron (Fe metal) — a moderately reactive metal displaces H₂ and gives the iron(II) salt.

(c) Barium nitrate: dilute nitric acid (HNO₃) + excess barium carbonate (BaCO₃) — barium metal is far too reactive; its insoluble carbonate is the safe route.

(d) Aluminium sulfate: dilute sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄) + excess aluminium (Al metal)

(e) Calcium chloride: dilute hydrochloric acid (HCl) + excess calcium carbonate (CaCO₃) — NOT calcium metal, the reaction is too vigorous.

(f) Zinc nitrate: dilute nitric acid (HNO₃) + excess zinc (Zn metal) / zinc oxide / zinc carbonate

Salt Preparation — Ex 2: Titration Method (Handout p13)

Suggest the reagents required to prepare the following soluble salts (all contain Group 1 or ammonium cations, so use the titration method with a dilute acid + dilute alkali).

(a) Ammonium nitrate: HNO₃(aq) + NH₃(aq)

(b) Potassium sulfate: H₂SO₄(aq) + KOH(aq)

(c) Lithium chloride: HCl(aq) + LiOH(aq)

(d) Sodium ethanoate: CH₃CO₂H(aq) + NaOH(aq)

(e) Potassium phosphate: H₃PO₄(aq) + KOH(aq)

Reagent-picking recipe: Match the anion to the acid (chloride → HCl, sulfate → H₂SO₄, nitrate → HNO₃, ethanoate → CH₃CO₂H, phosphate → H₃PO₄). Then match the cation: Group 1 / NH₄⁺ → its alkali (titration). Mg–Fe on the reactivity series → the metal itself works. Cu or very reactive metals → use the oxide, hydroxide or carbonate instead.

## Core reminders

blocks.title: Units first
blocks.body: Write SI units before substituting values into formulas.

blocks.markdown:
Eleven tabs, three topics. Start here if your brain has gone blank — these are the hooks that pull the rest of the topic back.

The 5 kinematics symbols

s u v a t

s = displacement u = initial velocity v = final velocity a = acceleration t = time

Every equation of motion uses four of these five. Write down the three you know and the one you want — the equation that contains exactly those four is the one to use.

Picking the right equation

MISSING LETTER

no s → v = u + at no v → s = ut + ½at² no t → v² = u² + 2as no a → s = ½(u+v)t

Ask "which quantity do I neither know nor need?" — then use the equation that leaves that letter out. No trial and error needed.

Reading motion graphs

SLOPE DOWN, AREA UP

gradient: s → v → a area: a → v → s

Going down the chain (displacement → velocity → acceleration) you take the gradient. Going back up you take the area under the graph. Two rules cover every graph question.

Newton's three laws

LAZY · FORMULA · FIGHT BACK

1st = Lazy (inertia) 2nd = Formula (F = ma) 3rd = Fight back (pairs)

1st: objects are lazy, they keep doing what they were doing. 2nd: unbalanced force gives the formula FR = ma. 3rd: push something and it pushes back, equally and oppositely.

Is it a true action–reaction pair?

MOBS

M = same Magnitude O = Opposite direction B = different Bodies S = Same nature

All four must hold. The classic trap: weight and normal force on a TV are not a pair — they act on the same body and are different natures (one contact, one non-contact).

Terminal velocity in one line

DRAG = WEIGHT

resultant force = 0 N a = 0 m s⁻² v = constant

Air resistance grows as speed grows. The moment it equals the weight, the forces balance — constant velocity, not zero velocity. Marks are lost every year for saying "it stops accelerating and slows down".

The six energy stores

Kangaroos Grab Elastic Chocolate In Nests

Kinetic Gravitational Elastic Chemical Internal Nuclear

Energy is stored in these six. Heat, light, sound and electricity are not stores — they are energy in transit, i.e. transfer pathways.

The four transfer pathways

M · H · W · E

Mechanically (force × distance) Heating (temperature difference) Waves (EM + sound) Electrically (current)

Energy moves between stores by exactly one of these four routes. Name the route and the two stores and you have a full-mark energy answer.

When is work done?

NO MOVE → NO WORK

W = F × s s is measured along the force

Carrying a box horizontally does zero work against gravity — the weight acts downwards but the box moves sideways, so the distance moved in the direction of the force is 0 m.

Mass vs weight

MATTER vs GRAVITY

Mass = amount of matter, kg, scalar Weight = force of gravity, N, vector

Your mass is the same on the Moon; your weight is about six times smaller because g falls from 10 N kg⁻¹ to 1.6 N kg⁻¹.

blocks.markdown:
The big idea: Kinematics describes how things move without asking why. Everything reduces to five quantities and a hard split between scalars (size only) and vectors (size and direction). Most lost marks in this topic come from swapping a vector for its scalar twin.

The quantity table

Quantity

Definition

SI unit

Type

metre (m)

The distance measured in a straight line from the starting point, in a stated direction

average speed = total distance ÷ total time · average velocity = net displacement ÷ total time · acceleration = (v − u) ÷ t

Distance vs displacement — the split that costs marks

Distance — scalar

Adds up everything you walked, no matter which way you turned. It can only ever increase. A full lap of a track gives a large distance.

Displacement — vector

Only cares where you ended up relative to where you started, plus a direction. It can decrease, and it can be zero. A full lap gives zero displacement.

Worked example — circular track Practice 1 Q1

An athlete runs half a lap of a circular track of radius 20 m, from A to the opposite point B, in 7.5 s.

(a) Average speed. Distance = half the circumference = 0.5 × π × (40 m) = 62.832 m.

Average speed = 62.832 m ÷ 7.5 s = 8.4 m s⁻¹ (2 s.f.)

(b) Magnitude of displacement A → B. The straight line from A to B is a diameter = 40 m.

(c) Why is average velocity zero over one complete lap? After one complete lap the athlete returns to his original position, so his net displacement is zero. Since velocity is displacement per unit time, a zero displacement gives a zero average velocity — even though his average speed is large.

Direction convention — the sign of the accelerationSpeeding up → acceleration is in the SAME direction as the velocity. Slowing down → OPPOSITE direction.velocity is +ve · Speeding upvaa is POSITIVEvelocity is +ve · Slowing downvaa is NEGATIVEvelocity is −ve · Speeding upvaa is NEGATIVEvelocity is −ve · Slowing downvaa is POSITIVEA negative acceleration does NOT always mean slowing down — it means the acceleration points the negative way.The direction of the axis you choose determines every sign in the question. State it before you calculate.

The sign of the acceleration depends on the direction of motion as well as on whether the object is speeding up or slowing down.

Exam traps to watch

The trapWhat the examiner wants instead

Writing "velocity = distance / time"

Velocity is displacement per unit time. Reserve "distance" for speed.

Giving a displacement with no direction

State the direction: "200 m, south of point A". A vector answer without a direction is incomplete.

Assuming negative acceleration always means slowing down

A negative sign only means "in the negative direction". An object speeding up in the negative direction also has negative acceleration.

Assuming constant speed means no acceleration

Moving in a circle at constant speed still means the direction of velocity is changing, so the object is accelerating.

Rounding too early

Keep full precision through the working; round only the final answer, and match the significant figures of the data (usually 2 or 3 s.f.).

Describing motion with diagrams

Ticker-tape timer — dot spacing shows how speed changesDots are printed at equal time intervals, so spacing = distance travelled per unit time.direction of motionConstant spacingConstant speeddirection of motionIncreasing spacingSpeeding updirection of motionDecreasing spacingSlowing downFree fall shows as steadily increasing spacing — constant acceleration of about 10 m s⁻².

Dot spacing on a ticker tape is a direct read-out of how the speed is changing.

A coin tossed at 20 m s⁻¹ and caught again — the same motion, four graphstime / svelocity / m s⁻¹20−2024straight line, crosses zero at 2 stime / sspeed / m s⁻¹2024V shape — speed can never be negativetime / sdisplacement / m2024returns to 0 m — back in the handtime / sdistance / m204024keeps rising to 40 m — never decreasesAt the top (t = 2 s) the velocity is zero but the acceleration is still −10 m s⁻² — the velocity line has no kink.

One motion, four graphs. Velocity goes negative; speed and distance never do.

Area under the line = displacement.

Every velocity–time shape in the syllabus. Note the fourth uniform case: speeding up in the negative direction is NOT deceleration.

Velocity–time graphs

ShapeWhat it meansHow to read it

Horizontal line above the axisConstant velocityGradient = 0, so acceleration = 0 and the forces are balanced.

Straight sloping lineUniform accelerationa = gradient = (v − u) ÷ t. The equations of motion are valid here.

Curve flattening towards a horizontal lineApproaching terminal velocityAcceleration decreasing to zero as air resistance builds up to equal the weight.

Line crossing the time axisThe object reversed directionAbove axis and below axis are opposite directions. Areas on opposite sides cancel when finding displacement.

Area under the lineDisplacementSplit into triangles and rectangles: triangle = ½ × base × height, rectangle = base × height.

Sketching the skydiver Practice 2 Q2

A skydiver reaches a terminal velocity of 55.6 m s⁻¹ after 10.0 s, falls for 70.0 s, opens her parachute and quickly slows to a new terminal velocity of 10.2 m s⁻¹, then lands 105 s later.

Stage 1 — 0 to 10 s: a steep curve rising from the origin and flattening, because air resistance increases as speed increases, so acceleration decreases.

Stage 2 — 10 s to 80 s: a horizontal line at 55.6 m s⁻¹. Air resistance now equals weight, resultant force is 0 N.

Stage 3 — parachute opens: a steep drop that curves and levels out at 10.2 m s⁻¹ — the larger cross-sectional area gives much greater air resistance, so there is a large upward resultant force and a deceleration that shrinks to zero.

Stage 4: horizontal at 10.2 m s⁻¹ until she lands.

Why the equations of motion cannot be used here: the acceleration is not uniform for parts of the journey, and the kinematics equations are only valid for uniform acceleration.

Marks are awarded for the boring things. In a sketch question the three marks usually go to: (1) axes labelled with quantity and unit, (2) correct shape including curvature, (3) key values marked on both axes. Draw the shape first, then go back and label.

Comparing the two graph types

Displacement–time vs velocity–time: one journeyA → B accelerating from restB → C constant velocityC → D decelerating to a stoptime / sdisplacement / mABCDconcave curvestraight lineconvex curvetime / svelocity / m s⁻¹ABCDgradient +ve constanthorizontalgradient −ve constantThe y-axis label tells you which graph you are reading. Check it first.

One journey, both graphs. The y-axis label tells you which you are reading.

Reading area off a velocity–time graph

Area under a velocity–time graph = displacementtime / svelocity / m s⁻¹0123451020304050Acceleration = gradient= (50 − 0) ÷ (5 − 0)= 10 m s⁻²0 s to 5 s — triangle= 0.5 × 5 × 50= 125 m4 s to 5 s — trapezium= 0.5 × (30 + 50) × 1= 40 mThe handout labels the gradient “velocity” here — it is the acceleration. The number is right, the label is not.

Gradient gives acceleration; area gives displacement. Split into triangles and trapeziums.

The skydiver, stage by stage

Skydiver — velocity–time graph with the four stagestime / svelocity / m s⁻¹55.610.21accelerating,2terminal velocity3parachute opens4new terminal velocity1Air resistance grows with speed, so the acceleration decreases — the curve flattens.2Air resistance = weight. lessons.title: Equations of Motion
lessons.summary: Choose and apply SUVAT equations for constant acceleration.

blocks.markdown:
## Four equations

- $v = u + at$
- $s = ut + \frac12at^2$
- $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$
- $s = \frac{u+v}{2}t$

Health warning: these four equations are only valid when the acceleration is uniform (constant). If a question mentions terminal velocity, a parachute or "changing acceleration", the equations do not apply for that stage — use a graph instead.

The four equations

v = u + at

leaves out s

Use when you don't know and don't want the displacement.

s = ut + ½at²

leaves out v

Use when the final velocity is neither given nor asked for.

v² = u² + 2as

leaves out t

Use when time is not mentioned anywhere in the question.

s = ½(u + v)t

leaves out a

Use when acceleration is unknown but both velocities are given.

How to attack any EOM question

1. Choose a positive direction and write it down. "Taking downwards as positive" earns nothing on its own but prevents almost every sign error.

↓

2. List s, u, v, a, t. Write the three you know, put a "?" on the one you want, and cross out the fifth.

↓

3. Pick the equation missing the crossed-out letter. Substitute with units, then solve.

↓

4. Sanity-check the sign and size. A car should not decelerate at 400 m s⁻², and a dropped ball should not have negative downward velocity.

Free fall

SituationWhat to use

Released from restu = 0, a = g. With g = 10 m s⁻²: s = ½gt² and v = gt.

Thrown upwardsTake up as positive: a = −g throughout, including at the very top. At maximum height v = 0 but a is still −g.

Air resistance negligibleAll objects fall with the same acceleration regardless of mass — a heavier nail takes exactly the same time to fall as a lighter one.

Air resistance significantAcceleration decreases as speed increases; the object may reach terminal velocity. EOM no longer valid.

Worked example — block down a ramp Practice 2 Q1

A block is released from rest and slides down a frictionless ramp 5.0 m long, reaching the end 1.6 s later.

(a) Velocity at the end of the ramp. Known: s = 5.0 m, u = 0, t = 1.6 s. Wanted: v. Missing: a → use s = ½(u + v)t.

5.0 = 0.5 × v × 1.6 → v = 6.3 m s⁻¹ (2 s.f.)

(b) Acceleration. Known: s, u, t. Wanted: a. Missing: v → use s = ut + ½at².

5.0 = 0 + ½ × a × (1.6)² → a = 3.9 m s⁻² (2 s.f.)

(c) Average speed for the whole journey (5.0 m on the ramp in 1.6 s, then 5.0 m on a rough surface in 3.2 s):

average speed = total distance ÷ total time = 10.0 m ÷ 4.8 s = 2.1 m s⁻¹ (2 s.f.)

Worked example — the Mars descent Dynamics Practice Q2

A 250 kg probe fires reverse thrusters at 40 m s⁻¹ and lands 30 s later at 0.75 m s⁻¹. Take gMars = 4.0 N kg⁻¹, no air resistance.

Step 1 — acceleration. Taking downwards as positive: a = (v − u) ÷ t = (0.75 − 40) ÷ 30 = −1.31 m s⁻² (i.e. a deceleration).

Step 2 — resultant force. FR = ma = 250 × (−1.31) = −327 N, so there is a resultant force of 327 N upwards.

Step 3 — bring in the weight. Weight = mg = 250 × 4.0 = 1000 N downwards.

1000 − thrust = −327 → thrust ≈ 1.3 × 10³ N upwards.

Why this is a two-topic question: kinematics gives you a, then Newton's second law converts a into a force. Almost every Sec 3 dynamics problem has this shape.

Free fall — reading g off the graph

Free fall — gradient of the speed–time graph gives gtime / svelocity / m s⁻¹123456710203040506070806 s60 m s⁻¹Gradient = acceleration= 60 ÷ 6g = 10 m s⁻²Free fall = the only forceacting is the weight.All objects fall at the samerate when there is no airresistance, whatever theirmass or size.Released from the sameheight, they land together.

The gradient of the speed–time graph for a freely falling body is g = 10 m s⁻².

lessons.title: Forces, Mass & Weight
lessons.summary: Use force diagrams and distinguish mass from weight.

blocks.markdown:
## Weight

$W = mg$. Mass is measured in kilograms and does not change with location. Weight is a force measured in newtons.

Definition to memorise: a force is a push or a pull on an object due to an interaction with another object. A force can make an object start moving, stop, speed up, slow down, or change direction — the "change in motion" phrase is what examiners look for.

The two families of force

Contact forces — objects must touch

Friction — opposes, or tends to oppose, motion between surfaces in contact.

Air resistance — the frictional force exerted by air that opposes the motion of a moving object.

Normal force — the push exerted by a surface on an object pressing on it, always perpendicular to the surface.

Tension — the pull exerted by a stretched spring, string or rope on an object attached to it.

Non-contact forces — act at a distance

Gravitational force — the pull exerted by the Earth's gravity on any object with mass. This is the object's weight.

Electrostatic force — attraction between unlike charges, repulsion between like charges.

Magnetic force — attraction between unlike poles, repulsion between like poles.

Mass vs weight

MassWeight

The amount of substance (matter) in the bodyThe force of gravity acting on the body

Constant in any locationDepends on the gravitational field strength at that location

Measured in kilograms (kg)Measured in newtons (N)

ScalarVector — it acts downwards, towards the centre of the Earth

Measured with a beam balance / electronic balanceMeasured with a spring balance (newton meter / force meter)

Gravitational field and field strength

W = mg · weight (N) = mass (kg) × gravitational field strength (N kg⁻¹)

TermDefinition you should be able to write out

Gravitational fieldA region in which a mass experiences a force due to gravitational attraction.

Gravitational field strength, gThe gravitational force per unit mass placed at that point. Unit: N kg⁻¹.

On Earthg ≈ 10 N kg⁻¹ — a 1 kg mass experiences a gravitational force of 10 N.

On the Moong ≈ 1.6 N kg⁻¹ — the same 1 kg mass experiences only 1.6 N.

Numerically equal to…the acceleration of free fall for a body near the Earth, which is why 10 N kg⁻¹ and 10 m s⁻² are interchangeable.

Density carried over from LSS

density = mass ÷ volume · SI unit kg m⁻³ · 1.0 g cm⁻³ = 1000 kg m⁻³

Floats

An object placed in a liquid of higher density than its own will float.

Sinks

An object placed in a liquid of lower density than its own will sink.

Unit conversion, done slowly once: 1 g cm⁻³ = (1/1000 kg) ÷ (1/1 000 000 m³) = 1000 kg m⁻³. Multiply g cm⁻³ by 1000 to get kg m⁻³; divide to go back.

lessons.title: Newton’s Laws & Free-Body Diagrams
lessons.summary: Explain motion using resultant force and action-reaction pairs.

blocks.markdown: Resultant force equals mass times acceleration: $F = ma$.
Forces in a pair are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, and act on different objects.

Newton's Laws & Free-Body Diagrams

Newton's first law

An object at rest will remain at rest, and an object in motion will continue to move at constant velocity, unless a resultant force acts on it.

If the forces are…Then the object…

Balanced (resultant force = 0 N)is in equilibrium: either at rest, or moving in a straight line at constant speed. Acceleration = 0 m s⁻².

Unbalanced (resultant force ≠ 0 N)accelerates in the direction of the resultant force — speeding up, slowing down, or changing direction.

The classic exam statement: "If the forces acting on an object are balanced, then the object must not be accelerating." It may well be moving — non-zero velocity does not mean non-zero resultant force. A 2 kg object gliding at 4 m s⁻¹ needs 0 N of resultant force to keep going.

Inertia — why the first law feels the way it does

IdeaExplanation

InertiaThe reluctance of a body to change its state of rest or motion. Newton's first law is also called the law of inertia.

Quantified by massThe greater the mass, the greater the inertia — a more massive object is harder to start, speed up, slow down or turn.

Seat beltsIn a collision a passenger in motion continues to move forward because of inertia. The seat belt exerts an external force on the passenger, decelerating them safely.

Box on an accelerating lorryThe box tends to stay where it was, so relative to the lorry it slides towards the back. When the lorry brakes, the box slides towards the front.

Passenger on a trainAs the train accelerates forwards, a frictionless passenger stays at rest relative to the ground, so she appears to move backwards relative to the train.

Newton's second law

The resultant force acting on an object is equal to the product of its mass and its acceleration, and the object accelerates in the direction of the resultant force.

FR = ma · FR = resultant force (N), m = mass (kg), a = acceleration (m s⁻²)

1 N is the force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m s⁻², so 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻².

Finding the resultant forceA · PARALLEL FORCES — add or subtract8 N → 2 N ←6 N →8 N → 2 N →10 N →8 N → 8 N ←no net forceB · PERPENDICULAR — Pythagoras4 N3 N5 N37° E of NC · STATIC POINT MASS, 3 FORCES — closed vector triangle5 N3 N3rd forceThe three forces are balanced, so thevectors form a CLOSED LOOP.Follow the arrows head to tail all the wayround — if you can trace one continuouscircuit, the triangle is drawn correctly.This is the preferred method: it gives thethird force directly, with no need to findthe resultant of the other two first.

Parallel, perpendicular, and the closed vector triangle for three balanced forces.

Finding the resultant force

CaseMethod

Parallel forcesSimple addition (same direction) or subtraction (opposite directions). Choose a positive direction first.

Perpendicular forcesPythagoras for the magnitude, trigonometry for the direction. 3 N east + 4 N north gives 5 N at 37° east of north.

Non-parallel forcesDraw to scale using the tip-to-tail method or the parallelogram method, then measure — or calculate with trigonometry.

Static point mass, 3 forcesThe forces are balanced, so the three vectors form a closed vector triangle — the three arrows follow each other head to tail in a closed loop. (Preferred method.)

Free-body diagrams — forces ON the object onlyW = weight N = normal contact force T = tension f = friction R = air resistanceTWHanging at rest from a stringNWResting on a horizontal surfaceWone force onlyFalling, no air resistanceRWarrows EQUAL lengthFalling at terminal velocityNfWN is ⊥ to the SLOPEAt rest on a rough slopeTWT longer than WPulled up, acceleratingNever draw the force the object exerts on the table, ground or rope — that acts on a different body.Label every arrow as “type of force on OBJECT by SOURCE”, and start the weight arrow at the centre of gravity.

Six standard free-body diagrams. Only forces acting ON the object appear.

Free-body diagrams

What it isA diagram showing the object (as a dot, a block or a sketch) and only the forces acting on it.

Rule 1 — forces ON the object onlyForces the object exerts on its surroundings must not appear. Half of all lost marks live here.

Rule 2 — label every arrow fullyUse "type of force on object by source", e.g. "normal contact force on box by table".

Rule 3 — start the arrow from the right placeWeight acts from the centre of gravity; normal force acts from the contact surface.

Rule 4 — arrow length shows magnitudeIf the object is in equilibrium, opposing arrows must be drawn the same length.

Action–reaction pairs — the TV on the tableTVN normal force on TV by tableW gravitational force on TV by EarthN′ normal force on table by TVGenuine pairsW pairs with gravitational force on the Earth by the TV✓both gravitational, different bodiesN pairs with normal force on the table by the TV (N′)✓both contact, different bodiesNOT a pairW and N — the weight of the TV and the normal force on the TVThey act on the SAME body, and they are of DIFFERENT natures (one non-contact, one contact).MOBS — equal Magnitude · Opposite direction · different Bodies · Same nature. All four must hold.

The TV on the table: two genuine action–reaction pairs, and the pair that is not one.

Newton's third law

If body A exerts a force on body B, then body B exerts an equal and opposite force on body A. Forces always occur in action–reaction pairs.

All four must be trueCheck

Equal in magnitudeSame size, always — even when a lorry hits a mosquito.

Opposite in directionExactly antiparallel.

Acting on different bodiesThis is the one that catches people out. One force on A, one force on B.

Of the same natureBoth contact, or both gravitational — never one of each.

The naming convention that guarantees the mark: write "[$type of force] by [$object exerting] on [$object experiencing]". Then the partner force is the same sentence with the two objects swapped. Swimming: "contact force by the wall on the boy" pairs with "contact force by the boy on the wall".

The TV on the table — the trap everyone falls into

A TV rests on a table. Four forces are in play: the gravitational force on the TV by the Earth (FET), the gravitational force on the Earth by the TV (FTE), the normal force on the TV by the table (n), and the normal force on the table by the TV (n′).

Genuine pairs: FET with FTE (both gravitational, different bodies) and n with n′ (both contact, different bodies).

NOT a pair: the weight of the TV and the normal force on the TV. They act on the same body and are of different natures (one non-contact, one contact). They happen to be equal here only because the TV is in equilibrium.

Why doesn't the Earth move towards a falling ball? The force on the Earth by the ball equals the force on the ball by the Earth, but since a = F/m and the Earth's mass is enormous, the Earth's acceleration is negligible.

lessons.title: Friction & Terminal Velocity
lessons.summary: Explain resistance forces and terminal velocity.

blocks.markdown: As speed rises, drag rises. Terminal velocity occurs when drag equals weight, so resultant force and acceleration are zero.

blocks.text: Terminal velocity — how the forces change

blocks.markdown:
The weight NEVER changes. Only the air resistance grows — until at stage 3 it equals the weight.

Resultant force = 0 N → acceleration = 0 m s⁻² → CONSTANT velocity, not zero velocity.

Definition: friction is the force that opposes, or tends to oppose, relative motion between two surfaces in contact. The "tends to" matters — friction acts on a stationary box you are pushing but failing to move.

Friction is not the enemy

Useful effectsUnwanted effects

Friction between shoes and the ground lets you walk without slipping; between tyres and road it lets cars accelerate, turn and brake.

Surfaces heat up, causing wear and tear on moving parts.

Friction lets a belt drive a pulley, a nail hold in wood, and a car park on a slope without sliding.

In machinery friction reduces efficiency, because a large amount of energy is transferred away as unwanted internal energy.

Ways to reduce friction

Ball and roller bearings between moving parts · surfaces separated by a lubricant · surfaces separated by an air cushion · smoother, streamlined shapes.

What friction depends on

The materials in contact · the roughness of the surfaces · it is proportional to the force pressing the surfaces together · and it is independent of the area of contact.

Terminal velocity — the four-stage story

Stage 1 — just releasedAir resistance is zero, so the only force is the weight. The resultant force is at its maximum and the object accelerates at g.

↓

Stage 2 — speeding upAs speed increases, air resistance increases. The resultant force (weight − air resistance) shrinks, so the acceleration decreases — the object is still speeding up, just less quickly.

↓

Stage 3 — terminal velocity reachedAir resistance has grown until it equals the weight. Resultant force = 0 N, acceleration = 0 m s⁻², and the object falls at a constant velocity.

↓

Stage 4 — parachute opensCross-sectional area jumps, so air resistance jumps above the weight. Now there is a resultant force upwards: the object decelerates until air resistance falls back to equal the weight, giving a new, lower terminal velocity.

The weight never changes; only the air resistance grows, until it balances the weight.

What changes the size of the terminal velocity

Mass of the falling object

A heavier object generally has a greater terminal velocity. Its weight is larger, so it must accelerate to a higher speed before air resistance can grow large enough to balance that weight.

Cross-sectional area

A larger area (an open parachute, a spread-eagled skydiver) experiences greater air resistance at any given speed, so the balance point comes sooner — a lower terminal velocity.

Model answer for "explain what is meant by terminal velocity" [1]: it is the constant velocity of a falling object reached when the air resistance on the object is equal to the gravitational force (weight) on it. Say "constant velocity", not "maximum speed", and always name both forces.

lessons.title: Work, Energy & Power
lessons.summary: Calculate work, power, efficiency, and energy changes.

blocks.markdown:
The model: energy sits in stores and moves between them along pathways. It is never created or destroyed. The SI unit for energy and for work is the joule (J), and both are scalars.

The six energy stores

StoreAlso calledExample

Kinetickinetic energyAny object in motion with speed v

Gravitational potentialgravitational potential energyAn object raised above the ground

Elastic potentialelastic potential energyA stretched rubber band, a compressed spring

Chemical potentialchemical potential energyFood, fossil fuels, batteries

Internalinternal energyA hot object — the KE and PE of all its molecules

Nuclearnuclear energyThe nuclei of atoms; released by fission

Vocabulary that loses marks: heat, light, sound and electricity are not stores — they are energy in transit. Avoid "heat energy", "sound energy", "light energy" and "electrical energy". Say internal energy (or just "heat" as a transfer), and energy transferred by sound waves / electrically. Also do not mix the two models: stores are transferred, forms are converted.

Energy stores and transfer pathwaysEnergy sits in STORES and moves along PATHWAYS. Name both stores and the pathway for full marks.THE SIX STORESKineticGravitationalpotentialElasticpotentialChemicalpotentialInternalNuclearTHE FOUR PATHWAYSMechanicallyby a force over a distanceBy heatingdue to a temperature differenceBy waveselectromagnetic and soundElectricallyby an electric currentEXAMPLE · a bulb in a circuitChemical storeof the dry cellelectricallyInternal storeof the bulbby wavesSurroundingslight + infraredHeat, light, sound and electricity are NOT stores — they are energy in transit. Avoid “heat energy”, “sound energy”, “light energy”.Stores are TRANSFERRED; forms are CONVERTED. Do not mix the two models in one sentence.

Six stores, four pathways, and one worked transfer chain.

The two formulas you must recall

EK = ½mv²

kinetic store

m in kg, v in m s⁻¹. Only the speed is squared — a very common slip.

EP = mgh

gravitational potential store

h is the height relative to the chosen reference level, usually the ground.

The four transfer pathways

PathwayExample

Mechanically, by a force acting over a distanceA force pushes a cart over a distance s, transferring energy to the cart's kinetic store.

By heating, due to a temperature differenceA hot pan transfers energy to the internal store of the butter, which melts.

By propagation of waves (electromagnetic and mechanical)Infrared from the Sun warms skin; sound waves from cymbals set eardrums vibrating.

Electrically, by an electric currentA dry cell transfers energy from its chemical potential store to the internal store of a bulb filament.

Principle of conservation of energy

(i) Energy cannot be created or destroyed. (ii) It can only be transferred from one store to another. (iii) The total energy of an isolated system is constant. (An isolated system is one that exchanges neither matter nor energy with its surroundings.)

Worked example — parcel down a smooth ramp

A 4.0 kg parcel slides down a smooth curved ramp from a height of 5.0 m. Take g = 10 m s⁻². Find the speed at the bottom.

By the principle of conservation of energy: loss in gravitational potential store = gain in kinetic store.

mgh = ½mv² → since the mass appears on both sides, it cancels: (10)(5.0) = ½v²

v = 10 m s⁻¹ — and notice the answer is independent of mass, which is why this is a favourite exam question.

Work done

W = F × s · work done = force × distance moved in the direction of the force · unit: joule (J)

SituationWork done by that force

Lifting a 50 N box through 1.1 mPositive: W = 50 × 1.1 = 55 J

Carrying the same box 2.0 m horizontally at constant speedZero: the weight acts downwards but there is no vertical displacement, so W = 50 × 0 = 0 J

Your hand stopping a ball you catchNegative: the force on the ball is opposite to the ball's displacement, so the hand removes energy from the ball's kinetic store.

Work done = force × distance moved IN THE DIRECTION of the forcePOSITIVE workLifting a 50 N box through 1.1 msFW = 50 × 1.1 = 55 Jforce and displacement in the SAME directionZERO workCarrying the box 2 m horizontallysW90° apartW = 50 × 0 = 0 Jdisplacement is PERPENDICULAR to the weightNEGATIVE workYour hand stopping a ball you catchsFW is negativeforce and displacement are OPPOSITENo work is done when the distance moved in the direction of the force is zero — carrying a box on the level does no work against gravity.

Positive, zero and negative work — decided by the direction of the displacement relative to the force.

Work–energy theorem

FR × s = ½mv² − ½mu² · the work done by the resultant force equals the change in the kinetic store.

Power

P = W ÷ t

work done per unit time

Power is the work done, or energy transferred, per unit time. Unit: J s⁻¹ = watt (W). Scalar.

P = F × v

force × velocity

A powerful machine is both strong (big force) and fast (big velocity). Handy for engines and jets.

Efficiency

efficiency = (useful energy output ÷ total energy input) × 100%

where total energy input = useful energy output + non-useful (wasted) energy

Worked example — the electric motor

An electric motor lifts a 10 N load through 5.0 m using 65 J of electrical input.

Useful output = work done on the load = 10 N × 5.0 m = 50 J.

Energy wasted = 65 − 50 = 15 J.

Efficiency = (50 ÷ 65) × 100% = 77%.

Efficiency is never 100% because some energy is always transferred to the internal store of the surroundings through friction and resistance.

lessons.title: Energy Resources & Singapore’s Trilemma
lessons.summary: Compare energy sources through reliability, affordability, and environmental impact.

items.title: Non-renewable
items.body: Reliable high output; finite and commonly produces emissions.

items.title: Renewable
items.body: Replenished naturally; output can be intermittent.

blocks.markdown:
Energy Resources & Singapore's Trilemma

Singapore's energy trilemma: as a small country with limited natural energy resources, Singapore has to balance energy security (supply that will not be disrupted), competitive pricing (affordable electricity), and environmental sustainability (renewable, low-impact resources). Almost every exam discussion question wants two of these three in tension.

Non-renewable — cannot be replenished, will run out

ResourceHow it worksAdvantagesDisadvantages

Fossil fuels

Have energy in the chemical potential store; burning transfers energy by heating to water, producing steam that drives turbines.

More reliable than weather-dependent resources; relatively cheap to produce.

Gases produced during burning cause environmental pollution and contribute to global warming.

Nuclear fuels

Uranium nuclei undergo fission, splitting into parts; energy moves from the nuclear store to the kinetic stores of those parts, heating water into steam.

Low-carbon, reducing greenhouse gas emissions; high reliability and uninterrupted supply.

Risk of accidents; pollution from improper disposal of radioactive waste.

Renewable — can be replenished

ResourceHow it worksAdvantagesDisadvantages

Biofuels

Ethanol, biodiesel and biogas derived from biomass; energy sits in the chemical potential store and is released by burning.

Widely available on a large scale; relatively cheap.

Burning still produces gases that contribute to global warming.

Wind

Energy in the kinetic store of the wind is transferred mechanically to the kinetic store of the turbine blades, which drive generators.

Renewable; clean — no harmful gases produced.

Intermittent — needs steady winds of about 20–25 km h⁻¹; noise pollution and loss of habitat.

Tides

Changing high and low tides rotate turbines below the water surface; kinetic store of water → kinetic store of turbines.

More reliable than wind or sun; clean.

High cost of building tidal barrages; marine life affected by altered currents and noise.

Hydropower

Water held behind a dam has energy in the gravitational potential store; releasing it transfers energy mechanically to the kinetic store of the water, spinning turbines.

Renewable and continually regenerated; clean.

High cost of dams; damming a river damages the surrounding environment.

Geothermal

Water reaching volcanic hotspots is heated under pressure, gaining energy in its internal store, and is forced up as steam to drive turbines.

Renewable; clean, naturally available energy.

Release of poisonous gases such as hydrogen sulfide during drilling; only available in certain regions.

Solar

Energy in the Sun's nuclear store travels as electromagnetic waves to solar panels made of semiconductors such as silicon, generating electricity.

Clean method of producing electricity; well suited to Singapore's high year-round irradiance.

Unavailable at night and weather-dependent; panels take up a lot of space.

Why not hydropower in Singapore? The height difference of the water source is the biggest contributor to the energy input of a hydroelectric plant, and Singapore has no large body of moving water with a drop of anything like 180 m. Solar is the sensible alternative: high average sunlight per unit area and plenty of flat, unobstructed rooftops.

lessons.title: Model Answer Guide — Physics Definitions
lessons.summary: Practise precise definitions and explanation structure.

blocks.markdown: Rate of change of velocity.
Constant speed reached when resultant force is zero.

Every definition and standard explanation from Kinematics, Dynamics and Work-Energy-Power, written the way the mark scheme wants it. Cover each completed response and state it before checking your answer.

A. Kinematics

Distance is the total length of path travelled by an object and is a scalar quantity. Displacement is the distance measured in a straight line from the starting point in a stated direction, and is a vector quantity.

Speed is the distance travelled per unit time, whereas velocity is the displacement per unit time. Acceleration is defined as the rate of change of velocity, and its SI unit is m s⁻².

After one complete lap an athlete returns to his original position, so his net displacement is zero. Since velocity is displacement per unit time, the average velocity is therefore also zero. The set of kinematics equations may only be used when the acceleration is uniform. In a skydiving question the acceleration is not uniform for parts of the journey, so the equations cannot be applied to those stages. On a displacement–time graph the gradient gives the velocity. On a velocity–time graph the gradient gives the acceleration and the area under the graph gives the displacement.

B. Forces, mass and weight

A gravitational field is a region in which a mass experiences a force due to gravitational attraction. Gravitational field strength, g, is defined as the gravitational force per unit mass placed at that point, and is measured in N kg⁻¹. Weight is the gravitational force acting on an object that has mass, calculated using W = mg. Mass is measured using a beam / electronic balance while weight is measured using a spring balance. Mass is constant in any location, whereas weight depends on g at that location.

Friction is the force that opposes, or tends to oppose, relative motion between two surfaces in contact. The frictional force is proportional to the force pressing the surfaces together and is independent of the area of contact.

C. Newton's laws

Newton's first law: an object at rest will remain at rest, and an object in motion will continue to move at constant velocity, unless a resultant force acts on it. When the forces on an object are balanced the resultant force is 0 N, the object is in equilibrium, and its acceleration is 0 m s⁻². It may still be moving, provided it moves in a straight line at constant speed.

Inertia is the reluctance of a body to change its state of rest or motion. It is quantified by the mass of the object: the greater this is, the greater the inertia.

Newton's second law: the resultant force acting on an object is equal to the product of its mass and its acceleration, and the object accelerates in the direction of the resultant force. One newton is the force that produces an acceleration of 1 m s⁻² when applied to a mass of 1 kg.

Newton's third law: if body A exerts a force on body B, then body B exerts an equal and opposite force on body A. For two forces to be an action–reaction pair they must be equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, acting on different bodies, and of the same nature.

The weight of a TV and the normal contact force on it are not an action–reaction pair because they act on the same body and are not of the same type of force (one contact, one non-contact). A free-body diagram shows the object and only the forces that act on it; the forces the object exerts on its environment should not appear.

D. Terminal velocity

As the speed of a falling object increases, the air resistance experienced by the object also increases. Terminal velocity is the constant velocity of a falling object reached when the air resistance on the object is equal to the gravitational force (weight) on the object. At terminal velocity the resultant force is 0 N and the acceleration of the object is 0 m s⁻². An object with a larger cross-sectional area experiences greater air resistance and therefore has a lower terminal velocity. A heavier object generally has a greater terminal velocity.

E. Work, energy and power

The principle of conservation of energy states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, but can only be transferred from one store to another, and that the total energy of an isolated system is constant. Work done by a constant force is defined as the product of the force and the distance moved in the direction of the force. Its SI unit is the joule and it is a scalar. No work is done when the distance moved in the direction of the force is zero. Negative work is done when the force and the displacement are opposite in direction.

The work–energy theorem states that the work done by the resultant force on a particle changes the energy in its kinetic store. Power is defined as the work done, or energy transferred, per unit time. Its SI unit is the watt, equal to one joule per second. Power may also be calculated as force × velocity. Efficiency is the useful energy output divided by the total energy input, expressed as a percentage. The total energy input equals the useful energy output plus the non-useful (wasted) energy.

Energy can be transferred by four pathways: mechanically by a force acting over a distance, by heating due to a temperature difference, by the propagation of waves, and electrically by an electric current.

1. List known quantities.
2. Select equation without an unnecessary unknown.
