4. Check significant figures and unit.
You are given a scenario. Your only job is to decide which approach you would reach for — no working out required. That decision is where most marks are actually won and lost.

The questions from your practices and worksheets, reduced to the method. If you can reproduce the first line of each one, the arithmetic follows.

1 · Two perpendicular forces Dynamics Practice Q1

A 4.0 N force acts due north on a 2.0 kg object at rest; a 3.0 N force pushes it due east.

Resultant force: the forces are perpendicular, so FR = √(4.0² + 3.0²) = 5.0 N, at an angle tan⁻¹(3.0/4.0) = 37° east of north.

(i) Acceleration: a = FR ÷ m = 5.0 ÷ 2.0 = 2.5 m s⁻², 37° east of north (same direction as the resultant force).

(ii) Velocity after 2.0 s: v = u + at = 0 + 2.5 × 2.0 = 5.0 m s⁻¹, also 37° east of north.

Marker's note: both answers are vectors — a magnitude alone will not score full marks.

2 · Velocity–time graph of a car Dynamics Practice Q3

A 1000 kg car speeds up from 0 to 5.0 m s⁻¹ in 5.0 s, cruises to 11.0 s, then decelerates. Road friction is 125 N.

(i) 0 – 5.0 s: a = gradient = 5.0 ÷ 5.0 = 1.0 m s⁻².

FR = ma → driving force − 125 = 1000 × 1.0 → driving force = 1125 N.

(ii) 5.0 – 11.0 s: constant velocity, so a = 0 and FR = 0.

driving force − 125 = 0 → driving force = 125 N.

The idea being tested: constant velocity does not mean no driving force — it means the driving force exactly balances friction.

3 · Two connected masses Dynamics Practice Q4

A 4.0 kg block is connected by a cable to a 2.0 kg block, which is pulled by a 20 N force. They move at a constant 3.0 m s⁻¹. Friction on the left block, F₁, is twice that on the right block, F₂.

Constant speed → a = 0 → resultant force on each block = 0. Take rightwards as positive.

Left block: T − F₁ = 0, so T = F₁ = 2F₂.

Right block: 20 − F₂ − T = 0, so T = 20 − F₂.

Solve: 2F₂ = 20 − F₂ → F₂ = 6.7 N, F₁ = 13 N, and the tension T = 13 N (2 s.f.).

4 · The school bag Dynamics Practice, O-Level Q10

A bag is pulled with force P against 0.5 N of friction; a graph of acceleration a against P is given, crossing the P-axis at 0.5 N.

(a) Why must P exceed 0.5 N? The applied force must be greater than the frictional force for the resultant force to be non-zero, so that the bag can accelerate.

(b)(ii) Finding m: at P = 2.0 N the resultant force = 2.0 − 0.5 = 1.5 N and the graph gives a = 0.75 m s⁻².

m = F ÷ a = 1.5 ÷ 0.75 = 2.0 kg. Do not take the gradient — the line does not pass through the origin, so a is not directly proportional to P.

(c)(i) v = u + at = 0 + 0.75 × 3.0 = 2.3 m s⁻¹.

(c)(ii) P reduced to 0.5 N: the resultant force becomes zero, so the acceleration is zero and the bag continues at a constant velocity of 2.3 m s⁻¹ (Newton's first law).

(d) Partner of P: the force acting on the student by the bag, equal in magnitude to P and opposite in direction.

5 · MRT carriages Worksheet 8 Q3

Two identical carriages move right at constant velocity; friction on each is 1.65 kN. The engine is in the right-hand (first) carriage.

Tension on the left carriage: net force = 0 → T − 1.65 = 0 → T = 1.65 kN.

Driving force: for the right carriage, −1.65 (tension) + driving force − 1.65 (friction) = 0 → 3.30 kN.

Accelerating case: with friction 2.00 kN each, mass 2000 kg each and a = 2 m s⁻², treat both carriages as one system:

driving force − 2 × 2000 = 4000 × 2.00 → driving force = 12 000 N.

General result for n carriages at constant velocity: driving force = nf, where f is the friction on one carriage.

6 · The Perseverance rover Worksheet 8 Q2

A 1000 kg rover is lowered at constant velocity onto Mars, where g = 3.721 m s⁻², by three ropes at equal angles.

Constant velocity → resultant force = 0. Total tension = weight = 1000 × 3.721 = 3721 N.

Per rope: 3721 ÷ 3 = 1240 N (4 s.f.).

Why a parachute helps: it increases the resistive force of air on the rover, creating a resultant force opposite to the motion, which reduces the acceleration of the descent. On a planet with no atmosphere it would do nothing, because there is no air to provide the resistive force.

If it were simply dropped from 25 m: v² = u² + 2as = 0 + 2(3.721)(25) → v = 14 m s⁻¹, which on impact would mean a force of order 10⁵ N — hence the ropes.

7 · The nail and the cork board WEP Practice Q1

A 10.5 g nail falls from rest through 80.0 cm and embeds 4.8 cm into a cork board.

(a) Would a heavier nail take longer? No — it takes the same time, because the acceleration due to gravity is independent of mass.

(b) Work done on the nail by the board. Total drop = 80.0 + 4.8 = 84.8 cm.

Loss in gravitational potential store = mgh = (0.0105)(10)(0.848) = 0.08904 J.

By conservation of energy the work done to stop the nail equals this loss → 0.089 J (2 s.f.).

(c) Average deceleration. W = Fd → F = 0.08904 ÷ 0.048 = 1.855 N.

a = F ÷ m = 1.855 ÷ 0.0105 = 180 m s⁻² (2 s.f.).

The trick: the height must include the 4.8 cm travelled inside the board, because the nail keeps falling while it decelerates.

8 · Car up an incline Worksheet 9 Q2

A 1500 kg car climbs to a height of 10.0 m on a 12.0° slope against 500 N of friction, with a driving force of 8.40 kN. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².

(a) Gain in gravitational potential store: mgh = 1500 × 9.81 × 10.0 = 147 kJ.

(b) Energy transferred away by friction: slope length = 10.0 ÷ sin 12.0° = 48.097 m; W = Fs = 500 × 48.097 = 24 000 J.

(c) Speed at 10.0 m: work done by engine = Fs = 8400 × 48.097 = 404 kJ.

By conservation of energy: 404 010 = 147 000 + EK + 24 000 → EK = 233 010 J → ½(1500)v² = 233 010 → v = 17.6 m s⁻¹.

Common error: using F = ma with only the driving force. Along a slope the component of the weight also acts, so the energy route is safer.

9 · The bouncing nickel ball Worksheet 9 Q3

A nickel sphere of radius 2.00 cm (ρ = 8.908 g cm⁻³) falls from 50.0 cm and rebounds to 30.0 cm.

Mass: m = ρV = 8.908 × (4/3)π(2.00)³ = 298.51 g = 0.29851 kg. Convert to SI units before substituting.

Work done by the gravitational field: mgh = 0.29851 × 9.81 × 0.500 = 1.46 J (3 s.f.).

Percentage energy loss on impact: since both energies are mgh with the same m and g, the masses cancel:

loss = (1 − h₂/h₁) × 100% = (1 − 30.0/50.0) × 100% = 40%.

Plausible observation: a loud sound is heard on impact — some energy in the kinetic store is transferred away by sound waves, which is why the ball cannot return to its original height.

10 · Motor and friction WEP Practice Q2

A battery supplies 500 J to a motor that pulls an object 40.5 m at constant speed with a 6.00 N force.

(a) Efficiency: useful energy = Fs = 6.00 × 40.5 = 243 J → efficiency = (243 ÷ 500) × 100% = 48.6%.

(b) Frictional force: by conservation of energy the wasted 500 − 243 = 257 J is the work done against friction → F = 257 ÷ 40.5 = 6.35 N.

Spot the inconsistency: at constant speed the frictional force should equal the 6.00 N driving force. The mismatch tells you the question's numbers are slightly off — noticing this is exactly the physical reasoning being trained.
